title: AI is redefining what an engineer is. The manager’s job is to make that identity bigger, not smaller.
summary: Waydev - AI is redefining what an engineer is. The manager's job is to make that identity bigger, not smaller.
body_markdown:
Leadership in the AI SDLC


AI is redefining what an engineer is. The manager’s job is to make that identity bigger, not smaller.


Anthropic CTO Rahul Patil recently shared an internal post about the most important thing he believes a manager can do: expand a person’s core identity. It is a leadership lesson for any era. In the AI SDLC, where engineers are watching agents take over work that used to define them, it might be the most important management skill there is.


AC


**Alex Circei** CEO and Co-Founder, Waydev


The lesson


## Three hours in a conference room


Patil describes a moment from early in his career. He was a young manager on an exceptional team, building software that still runs in production at enormous scale. Then customers delivered swift, harsh feedback about one commercial decision they hated. Nobody handled it well: not his manager, not him, not the team. He spent three hours alone in a conference room replaying everything, feeling small and alone, and decided he never wanted to feel that way again or see anyone else feel it.


“Expanding a person’s identity is the most important thing a manager can do.”


Rahul Patil, CTO at Anthropic, adding: especially in tough moments


His reasoning is worth sitting with. How we see ourselves, and what we believe we can do, is tightly linked to how we use our intelligence. When people feel their identity is under threat, much of their intelligence goes into protecting it. Help someone expand their identity, and you free that intelligence and passion for the actual mission.


Why now


## AI is the biggest identity shift engineering has faced


For decades, a software engineer’s identity was closely tied to writing code. Today, agents generate a growing share of it. Many engineers are quietly asking themselves a hard question: if an agent writes most of the code, what am I?


That is exactly the kind of identity threat Patil describes, and it shows up the same way. Engineers who feel smaller protect themselves. They resist new tools, avoid experiments that might fail in public, or adopt AI quietly without sharing what works. None of that is a technology problem. It is a management problem.


The opportunity is that the AI era genuinely makes the role bigger. As we wrote in[When code gets cheap, engineering judgment gets expensive](https://waydev.co/?p=23288) , the scarce skill is no longer typing code. It is deciding what should exist, verifying what agents produce, designing systems that hold up, and owning the outcome. A manager’s job is to help each engineer see themselves in that larger role.


The framework


## Patil’s three qualities, applied to the AI SDLC


Patil names three qualities of a great manager, each an opportunity to expand individual and collective identity. Here is how each one translates for engineering leaders managing teams through the shift to AI.


1


**Leadership** See around corners, inspire people to attempt the impossible, and earn the trust of those who believe in that future. In short: raise ambition and help people believe they can get there.


**In the AI SDLC:** paint a picture of what your team can build now that was impossible two years ago. Make it clear that the goal is bigger ambitions, not fewer engineers.


2


**Organizing for results** Be vulnerable enough to be wrong but confident enough to challenge the status quo. Trust teammates and accept help from unexpected places. Build in the open for rapid iteration. Accept that solving one bottleneck creates the next, and swarm to it.


**In the AI SDLC:** share AI experiments openly, including the ones that failed. Let the best prompts and workflows come from anyone. And use data to find where the bottleneck moved this month, not where it was last year.


3


**Being there for people** Commit to leaving every conversation with everyone’s identity expanded. Bigger does not mean comfortable: a tough conversation can still leave someone bigger if they walk out seeing who they can become.


**In the AI SDLC:** when an engineer’s role changes, say so directly and describe the bigger version of it. Honest is kinder than vague.


Swarm to the next bottleneck


## Solving one bottleneck creates the next


This line from Patil’s post describes the AI SDLC almost perfectly. AI removed much of the friction of writing code. The constraint did not disappear. It moved downstream, into review queues, testing, release, and the product decisions about what to build next.


Illustrative. Where the bottleneck sits differs by team, and it keeps moving.


Patil’s advice is to not take it personally when you miss a bottleneck, and to swarm to the next one. That is only possible if you can see it. Teams that track[code review flow](https://waydev.co/?p=8585) , verification time and rework alongside[AI adoption](https://waydev.co/how-to-measure-ai-adoption-across-large-engineering-organizations/) spot the new constraint in weeks. Teams without that visibility find out a quarter later, usually from a missed deadline.


Data and identity


## Metrics can make people bigger or smaller


This is where engineering intelligence and Patil’s principle meet. Data is powerful, and how it is used decides whether it expands or shrinks the people it describes. The same dashboard can be a tool for coaching or a tool for blame.


**METRICS THAT MAKE PEOPLE SMALLER** Individual leaderboards of lines of code or commits. AI usage tracked as surveillance. Numbers presented as verdicts. Activity counts that reward volume over judgment.


**METRICS THAT MAKE PEOPLE BIGGER** Team-level views of where work gets stuck. Data used to start conversations, not end them. Recognition for review quality, design and verification, not just output. Outcomes like quality and[AI ROI](https://waydev.co/how-to-measure-ai-roi-on-your-engineering-team/) measured at the system level.


Engineering data should help people see who they can become, not just what they did last sprint.


Alex Circei, CEO, Waydev


The test


## Bigger or smaller?


Patil ends with a simple reflection for new and experienced managers alike: after each meeting, ask whether people left with their identity bigger or smaller. An honest answer, he says, teaches you a lot about being the best people coach you can be, for others and for yourself.


We would add one more place to ask it. After every engineering metrics review, every AI rollout update and every performance conversation that uses data, ask the same question.


?


**Did the data point at a system, or at a person?** Bottlenecks live in processes. Start there.


?


**Did we recognize judgment, not just volume?** The engineer who caught a bad agent change created as much value as the one who shipped ten.


?


**Did people leave knowing what bigger looks like?** Every number should come with a picture of the next version of the team.

## The bigger version of engineering


Patil’s lesson is timeless, but its timing is perfect. AI will change what every engineer does in the next few years. Whether that change makes your people feel smaller or bigger is not up to the models. It is up to their managers, and to how those managers use every conversation, every review and every number in front of them.
